clue.text: Uncertainly peel off tape that's sticky … sweet!

indicators.note: done uncertainly, the job is fumbled and the letters come out in a muddled order

parts.note: the three words taken letter for letter as the material

explanation.surface: Someone fumbles at a strip of sticky tape, then exclaims at something sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition straddles the dots: the answer is the sticky sweet, and the eleven letters of PEEL OFF TAPE rearrange into TOFFEE APPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A toffee apple is a fruit coated in hard caramel on a stick, a famously tacky fairground treat.

clue.text: Getting tense over money — bother!

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
the rouble is the Russian currency

explanation.surface: Someone grows anxious about cash and mutters an exasperated oath.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue one piece sits over the next, so T stands on top of ROUBLE; 'money' is a specific currency here, not cash in general.
explanation.definitionFit: As nouns both mean difficulty or inconvenience, as in 'it was no trouble' or 'it was no bother'.

clue.text: Golfer calls this rugby player 'hairy bit at the front'

parts.note: golfers shout this warning before a ball flies towards people
a lock is a second-row forward in a rugby scrum

explanation.surface: A golfer nicknames a rugby player after his shaggy fringe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golfer calls this' clues the shouted warning, and a lock is one of the tall forwards in rugby's second row of the scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A forelock is the lock of hair growing just above the forehead, playfully described as a hairy part at the front.

clue.text: Show some of convex polyhedron

indicators.note: only a portion of the following run of letters is wanted, so the word sits inside them

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A geometry lesson displays part of a many-faced solid.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer bridges the two words: conv-EX PO-lyhedron.
explanation.definitionFit: An expo is a large public exhibition, a trade fair or exposition, which is a kind of show.

clue.text: In style of Bible stories (not about healing mathematician)

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to leave something out of the word that follows

parts.note: à la is French for 'in the style of'
NT is the New Testament, a set of Bible books
curing is healing
C is circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: It reads as a note on the style of Bible narratives, minus the miraculous cures.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like an aside but belongs to the wordplay, and 'not about' means drop the abbreviation for circa. Only the last word, outside it, is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Turing was the British mathematician who founded computer science and helped break the Enigma code in wartime.

clue.text: It's his historic fourth term: submit!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the Russian leader who won a fourth presidential term in 2018
second meaning: to hand in, as with an application or a claim

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration (3,2) splits the leader's surname into a phrasal verb; the first definition is a description of him, not of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Vladimir Putin began a historic fourth term as Russian president, and to put in a form is to submit it.

clue.text: Coming up in the Spanish-German city, Earl to get more distinguished

definitions.note: the answer is transitive, to make someone more distinguished

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: el is Spanish for 'the'
Bonn was the West German capital
E is the abbreviation for earl

explanation.surface: In a German city with Spanish connections, a nobleman is raised to higher rank.
explanation.walkthrough: EL, BONN and E are laid down in clue order and the whole string is then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To ennoble is to raise someone to the nobility or, more loosely, to lend them dignity and stature.

clue.text: Time and time again, freak out about time in water spent by King

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one item wraps the next
'in' places the built piece inside what follows

parts.note: wee-wee is a childish word for urine, water passed or spent

indicators.note: losing control means losing order, so the letters come out scrambled

parts.note: taken as written for rearranging
T is the abbreviation for time
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: Someone panics, again and again, about the time a monarch spends in the bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water spent' is the nursery word for urine, doubled. 'Time' appears twice: once in the definition, once as a single letter of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe something recurring repeatedly and relentlessly over a long stretch.

clue.text: Perhaps English eke out small amount to be eaten: that's ironic

parts.note: English is an example of a tongue, a language

indicators.note: something eked out is stretched and spread about, so these letters get rearranged
what is eaten gets swallowed into the mix, so another piece joins the jumbled letters

parts.note: an inch is a small measure, as in 'give an inch'
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A sarcastic remark about the English making a little food last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals an example: English is one language among many. The small amount is swallowed into the jumble rather than added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A tongue-in-cheek remark is said with mock seriousness, meaning something other than its literal words, which is irony.

clue.text: Got into regressive irrational spiritual teachings for self-aggrandizement

indicators.note: getting into something means going inside it
regressing is going backwards, so the letters run in the opposite direction

parts.note: pi is the best-known irrational number
RE is religious education, a school subject
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone takes up backward, irrational mysticism purely to feel important.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irrational' is a noun here, the most famous irrational number, and 'spiritual teachings' is the school subject of religious education.
explanation.definitionFit: An ego trip is an activity pursued chiefly to boost one's own sense of importance, so it is self-aggrandizement.

clue.text: Not tense at first, prepared notation for The Merchant of Venice

definitions.note: the title character, not the play

indicators.note: something prepared has been worked over and put into a new form
'not' tells us something is to be left out
it is only the earlier of two possible copies that goes

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: An actor, relaxed at first, prepares a marked-up script of Shakespeare's play.
explanation.walkthrough: NOTATION has two Ts; dropping the first leaves NOATION, which rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's play the merchant of the title is Antonio, who borrows from Shylock to help his friend Bassanio.

clue.text: Capital city of Alaska …?' '… Bullwinkle?'

indicators.note: the answer is made of what follows, drawn from within the text

parts.note: the end of the first word joins the start of the second across the dots

explanation.surface: A quiz exchange: one voice asks for Alaska's capital, another suggests a cartoon moose.
explanation.walkthrough: Bullwinkle is the moose of the American cartoon Rocky and Bullwinkle; the answer spans alas-KA BUL-lwinkle.
explanation.definitionFit: Kabul is the capital city of Afghanistan, so it fits the plain two-word definition.

clue.text: Freshened up … but king's malodorous creature

indicators.note: something freshened up has been rearranged and given a new look

parts.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tidied themselves up, yet the monarch still smells.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is ignored; 'malodorous' just means bad-smelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A stink bug is a shield bug that releases a foul odour when disturbed, so it is a smelly insect.

clue.text: Deplorable, the French historian's work

parts.note: chronic is British slang for very bad
les is French for 'the' before a plural

explanation.surface: A harsh review dismisses a French scholar's book as dreadful.
explanation.walkthrough: In British informal speech 'chronic' means dreadful, as in 'the service was chronic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chronicles are records of events in order of time, the typical output of a medieval historian.

clue.text: Cor, that's some brass!

parts.note: surface reading: a British exclamation of surprise, then a remark about someone's cheek or money
setter's reading: the italic word is the French name of a brass instrument, translated

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cor!' is British slang for 'gosh!', and brass is slang for nerve or cash; in French a cor is a horn, and the italics flag the foreign word.
explanation.definitionFit: The cor is the French word for horn, and this orchestral brass instrument is named for France in English.

clue.text: Starters of midye, ezme, zacuscă & enginar?

definitions.text: Starters of midye, ezme, zacuscă & enginar

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters

parts.note: first letter; midye are Turkish stuffed mussels
first letter; ezme is a spicy Turkish tomato salad
first letter; zacuscă is a Romanian vegetable spread
first letter; enginar is Turkish for artichoke, often served in olive oil

explanation.surface: A menu lists a spread of little Turkish and Balkan starter dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the first letters spell the answer, and the four dishes are themselves examples of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Meze are small appetiser dishes served together in Turkish, Greek and Balkan cooking, exactly what these four foods are.

clue.text: Plastic bag finally forsook for good (best)

indicators.note: one thing in place of another, swapped in for it

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the closing letter of the word beside it

parts.note: the closing letter of the word
G is the abbreviation for good
the elite are the best of a group

explanation.surface: Someone gave up plastic bags for good, which is the best thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For good' looks like 'permanently', but it means in place of the letter for good. The bracketed word is wordplay too, not an aside.
explanation.definitionFit: Bakelite was an early synthetic resin, widely used for radios and telephones, and is a type of plastic.

clue.text: Heidegger's regularly showing irritation

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the even letters of the philosopher's name

explanation.surface: The German philosopher is often irritable.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th letters of HEIDEGGER; the 's is just 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An edge in someone's voice is a sharp note of annoyance, so the word can stand for irritation.

clue.text: Creeps travel aimlessly in Golfs every now and then

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside the other
only occasional letters are used, at spaced intervals

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters
to rove is to wander

explanation.surface: Someone drifts around in Volkswagen Golfs now and then, being obsequious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creeps' is a verb, not the noun for unpleasant people.
explanation.definitionFit: To creep, in the sense of fawning on a superior, is to grovel, behaving with abject servility.

clue.text: Discovered Everyman wearing large amount of make-up

parts.note: found is discovered

indicators.note: whoever wears something is inside it

parts.note: a ton is a large amount
the setter refers to themself, as I

explanation.surface: The setter is caught out wearing heavy make-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym stands for I, which goes inside A TON.
explanation.definitionFit: Foundation is the base cosmetic spread over the skin before other make-up is applied.

clue.text: Progress with play, mostly sardonic

definitions.note: the answer is a plural noun, usually in 'make inroads'

indicators.note: most but not all of the word is used, so its last letter goes
letters at play move freely around

parts.note: the word without its final letter

explanation.surface: A theatre critic notes that a play is moving forward but mostly in a mocking tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like a noun for a drama, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Making inroads means advancing or gaining ground on a task, so inroads stands for headway.

clue.text: Crossword setter in ramshackle hut, down to make something with clues

indicators.note: a ramshackle structure is falling apart, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as I
both words taken as written

explanation.surface: A crossword setter, depressed in a tumbledown shack, works on a new puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Something with clues' sounds like a crossword, but it is a detective story full of clues.
explanation.definitionFit: A whodunit is a detective novel or play in which the reader follows the evidence to identify the culprit.

clue.text: Practice in America: 'grey' oddly seen

parts.note: USA is the abbreviation

indicators.note: odd-numbered positions are kept, the first, third and so on

parts.note: the first and third letters

explanation.surface: A note on American spelling: the word is written 'gray' there, so 'grey' looks odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Practice in America' looks like a spelling note (American 'practice' versus British 'practise'), but 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage means customary practice, the habitual way something is done or a word is employed.

clue.text: Planet's environment agreeably receptive to humans … initially

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the start, so opening letters are kept

parts.note: the opening letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A description of a world whose conditions happen to suit human life.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is'; the surface also describes the answer, which is home to humans.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth is the third planet from the Sun, the one people live on.

clue.text: Those on smartphones in part of church called out

indicators.note: something called out is spoken, so we go by its sound

parts.note: an apse is the semicircular recess at the east end of a church

explanation.surface: Worshippers are scolded for using their phones in church.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests people glued to their phones, but 'Those' are things on the phones.
explanation.definitionFit: Apps, short for applications, are the programs installed on a smartphone.

clue.text: Take a gander at cocktail in East End bar

indicators.note: in a London East End pub the word is said in a Cockney accent, which drops the H

parts.note: a highball is a long drink of spirits and mixer, said without its opening H

explanation.surface: Someone eyes up a cocktail in a pub in London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is the traditional Cockney part of London, where the H of HIGHBALL is dropped; 'gander' is slang for a look.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball something is to look at it closely, and taking a gander is British slang for having a look.

clue.text: Who's in charge of bishops? Big ape, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an archbishop presiding over the bishops of a province
second meaning: a mammal of the order including apes and monkeys

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks a big ape as one example of the animal group.
explanation.definitionFit: The senior archbishop of a country is its primate, and gorillas and chimpanzees belong to the zoological order of primates.

clue.text: Setter sips a little soup cooked for family members

indicators.note: cooked ingredients are mixed and transformed

parts.note: both words taken as written

indicators.note: just a tiny bit of the word, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: The setter tastes a spoonful of soup made for relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' looks like it describes the soup, but it is the anagram signal for all eleven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Stepsisters are daughters of a step-parent, so they are relatives by marriage within a family.
